newsitem.title: ITALY: Hard-left demands Italy govt deny pension cutback.
newsitem.headline: Hard-left demands Italy govt deny pension cutback.

text.p: Italy's hard-left Communist Refoundation party urged the government on Monday to deny reports it wanted to scrap early retirement for all state sector workers, saying it could not give its support if they were true.

Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said media reports that the government was considering blocking early pensions for civil servants were "exceptionally serious" and he called for "an immediate and definitive denial from the government".
He said that if the government was seeking to "call into question the right for all state sector employees to take early retirement, then the government will not be able to count on its majority.
"The opposition of Communist Refoundation would be very fierce," he said in a statement.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi relies on support from Bertinotti's party for a parliamentary majority and his government almost fell earlier this year when Refoundation withdrew its backing for a security force for Albania.
Prodi's centre-left government is fighting to control state spending to meet targets for the European single currency and has begun talks with union leaders over welfare reform.

Bertinotti has already announced his utter opposition to any cuts in state spending, but economists say Italy must tackle the thorny issue to have a hope of being in economic and monetary union at its 1999 launch.
Prodi's cabinet on Friday approved a plan to stem the flood of teachers seeking retirement, meaning that only around half of the 65,000 teachers who have requested it would be given the go-ahead.

A hold-down on early retirements could bring big savings for the cash-strapped Treasury. State pensions body Inps has reported a recent surge in early retirement requests from various sectors amid rising fears of a government crackdown on pension benefits.
Italy spends more than any other European Union country on pension benefits and the bill is set to climb unless reforms are introduced, the statistical institute Istat said last week.

While Italy's total welfare spending is lower than the European Union average, spending on old age pensions was 13 percent of gross domestic product in 1994, almost three percent more than the EU average, Istat said in its annual report.
